beats.beat: Farr walks the mile to Oakmere and finds smoke rising from the chimney and unfamiliar curtains in windows he remembers as his great-uncle's.
Hartwell greets him civilly from the doorstep but does not ask him in, calling his arrival a surprise rather than a homecoming.
Hartwell produces the later will, drawn weeks before Fenner's death and witnessed by two of the farm's own servants, leaving everything to himself.
Farr states that his great-uncle promised him the farm by word before he went for a soldier, and has no paper to prove it.
Turned from his own door, Farr walks back toward the village, watched from an upstairs window by the housekeeper, Mrs Whitlow, who says nothing.

turn.note: Whitlow's silent, watchful presence at the window plants the question of what she knows and why she won't say, which the mystery needs to move forward.

problems: The door shut. Not hard; that was the worst of it. — states a judgment about feeling rather than showing it.

generic_prose.quote: Not hard; that was the worst of it.
generic_prose.replace_with: Give a physical detail of the shutting — the click of the latch, or Farr's hand still half-raised as if to knock again.

generic_prose.quote: There was a pause of some length.
generic_prose.replace_with: Name the pause with something concrete — Hartwell turning the watch-chain, or the dog settling back on its haunches.

trope_note: Serves the disputed inheritance directly through the will's production, and sets up the returning officer's disbelieved claim; forced proximity is not yet in play, which is correct for this chapter.
